easy.prompt: Which of the following is a proposition (has a definite truth value)?
easy.hint: Next step: ask of each option whether it is true-or-false right now, without extra information.
easy.explanation: Only "2 + 3 = 5" is true-or-false on its own; commands, questions, and open expressions have no truth value.
easy.deepDive: A proposition must be declarative with a determinate truth value in context. Commands express orders and questions request information, so neither is true or false. An expression with a free variable like "x + 1" becomes a proposition only once x is specified or bound.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A command expresses an order, not a claim — it is never true or false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A question asks for information rather than asserting anything checkable.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: With x unspecified this is an open expression, not a true-or-false claim.

easy.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a proposition?
easy.hint: Next step: check which option fails to assert something that could be true or false.
easy.explanation: "What time is it?" is a question, so it has no truth value; the rest are declarative claims.
easy.deepDive: Propositions are declarative sentences with fixed truth values. Each of the other options asserts a checkable fact about geography, arithmetic, or color. Interrogatives never count, even when the answer is obvious.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This asserts a geographic fact that is true, so it is a proposition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: This asserts an arithmetic fact that is true, so it is a proposition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: This asserts a (normally true) claim about snow, so it is a proposition.

easy.prompt: Which of the following becomes a proposition only after extra information is supplied?

choices.label: A
choices.body: "She is in Calgary." (no referent for 'she' given)

easy.hint: Next step: look for the sentence whose truth depends on who 'she' refers to.
easy.explanation: Without a referent for 'she' the sentence has no fixed truth value; the others are true outright.
easy.deepDive: Indexicals and pronouns need context to pin down a claim. Once 'she' is fixed to a person, the sentence is a proposition. By contrast, pure arithmetic or definitional claims are already complete. This is why logicians distinguish sentences-in-context from bare sentence types.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is a complete arithmetic claim, true with no extra context needed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: This is true by definition of a circle, needing no referent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: This is a complete arithmetic claim about 2.

easy.prompt: Let P be false. What is the truth value of ¬¬P?
easy.hint: Next step: flip twice — first evaluate inner ¬P, then negate the result.
easy.explanation: ¬P flips false to true, and negating again flips back to false, so ¬¬P agrees with P.
easy.deepDive: Double negation cancels: ¬¬F = ¬T = F, and ¬¬T = ¬F = T. So ¬¬P ≡ P in every row. Single negation always disagrees with its input, but applying it twice returns home. This is why 'it is not the case that P is false' just says P.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the value after one flip (¬P), before the second negation flips it back.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Both flips are defined, so the result has a definite value: false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Classical formulas take exactly one value — here false.

easy.prompt: Let P be true and Q be false. What is the truth value of P ∧ Q?
easy.hint: Next step: recall ∧ needs BOTH sides true — check whether Q passes that test.
easy.explanation: Conjunction is true only when both conjuncts are true; here Q is false, so P ∧ Q is false.
easy.deepDive: The truth table for ∧ has exactly one true row: T∧T. Every other combination (T∧F, F∧T, F∧F) is false. So a single false conjunct sinks the whole conjunction. This strictness is what distinguishes 'and' from inclusive 'or'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would require both P and Q true; Q is false here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Classical propositions take exactly one truth value, never both.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P and Q each have values, so the compound has one too — it is false.

easy.prompt: Let P be false and Q be true. What is the truth value of P ∨ Q?

choices.label: C
choices.body: True only if P is also true

easy.hint: Next step: recall ∨ is inclusive — ask whether AT LEAST ONE side is true.
easy.explanation: Inclusive disjunction is true when at least one disjunct is true; Q is true, so P ∨ Q is true.
easy.deepDive: The ∨ table has exactly one false row: F∨F. All other rows are true, including mixed T/F cases. Everyday 'either/or' sometimes means exclusive, but logic's ∨ is inclusive. So one true disjunct suffices.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the rule for ∧ with a false input, not for ∨ with a true input.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That confuses ∨ with ∧; ∨ needs only one true side.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: With both inputs valued, the disjunction always has a value.

easy.prompt: Let P be false and Q be false. What is the truth value of P ∨ Q?

choices.label: C
choices.body: True, because opposites make a true 'or'

easy.hint: Next step: check whether AT LEAST ONE disjunct is true — here neither is.
easy.explanation: P ∨ Q is false exactly when both P and Q are false, which is the case here.
easy.deepDive: F∨F is the single false row of the disjunction table. Students sometimes think two falses 'cancel', but ∨ only reports whether a true option exists. With none present, the disjunction is false. Contrast ∧, whose single true row is T∧T.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nothing is true here, so inclusive 'or' cannot be true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Falses do not cancel under ∨; only a true disjunct makes it true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No classical formula is both true and false at once.

easy.prompt: Let P be true. What is the truth value of ¬P?
easy.hint: Next step: apply the flip rule — negation reverses the input value.
easy.explanation: Negation flips truth value, so ¬(true) is false.
easy.deepDive: The ¬ table has just two rows: ¬T = F and ¬F = T. Negation is a flip, not a preserver. Double negation flips twice and returns the original, which is why ¬¬P ≡ P. Single negation always disagrees with its input.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That keeps P's value instead of flipping it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Negation never agrees with its input — that describes double negation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Classical negation yields exactly one value, the opposite one.

easy.prompt: Let P be false and Q be true. What is the truth value of ¬P ∧ Q?

choices.label: C
choices.body: False, because negation makes everything false

easy.hint: Next step: evaluate inside-out — first flip P, then check the ∧.
easy.explanation: ¬P flips false to true, and true ∧ true is true, so the whole formula is true.
easy.deepDive: Order of evaluation matters: ¬ binds tightest, so compute ¬P = T first. Then the conjunction T∧T yields T. A common slip is to carry P's falsity through the negation. Instead, always finish the ¬ before judging the ∧.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: P's falsity was already flipped by ¬ before the ∧ was evaluated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Negation flips a value; it does not force falsity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both inputs are valued, so the compound has a definite value.

easy.prompt: How many rows does the truth table of a formula with 2 distinct atomic propositions have?
easy.hint: Next step: each new letter doubles the rows — compute 2^2.
easy.explanation: Each of the 2 letters can be T or F independently, giving 2^2 = 4 rows.
easy.deepDive: A truth-table row is a valuation: an assignment of T/F to each atom. With n atoms there are 2^n valuations, since each atom doubles the possibilities. For n = 2 the rows are TT, TF, FT, FF. Adding a third atom would double again to 8.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That counts the values per atom, not the combinations across 2 atoms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That adds or multiplies instead of exponentiating — rows grow as 2^n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is 2^3, the count for three atoms, not two.

easy.prompt: How many rows does the truth table of a formula with 3 distinct atomic propositions have?
easy.hint: Next step: apply 2^n with n = 3.
easy.explanation: With 3 atoms there are 2^3 = 8 valuations, hence 8 rows.
easy.deepDive: List them systematically: TTT, TTF, TFT, TFF, FTT, FTF, FFT, FFF. Each of the 4 two-atom rows splits in two when the third atom varies. Guesses like 6 (2×3) or 9 (3^2) confuse multiplication with the doubling rule. Only exponentiation captures independent binary choices.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That multiplies 2×3 instead of exponentiating 2^3.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That computes 3^2, swapping base and exponent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That counts atoms, not combinations of their values.

easy.prompt: A formula uses 4 distinct atomic propositions. How many truth-table rows does it need?
easy.hint: Next step: double the 3-atom count (8) once more for the fourth atom.
easy.explanation: 2^4 = 16 rows — each added atom doubles the previous count.
easy.deepDive: The doubling recurrence is R(0) = 1, R(n+1) = 2·R(n), giving R(n) = 2^n. So 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 for n = 0..4. Answer 8 forgets to double for the fourth atom. Linear guesses like 12 (4×3) miss the exponential growth that makes brute-force tables infeasible for large n.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the 3-atom count — you must double once more for the fourth atom.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That multiplies instead of exponentiating.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That counts atoms rather than valuations.

easy.prompt: In which row is P ∧ Q true?
easy.hint: Next step: scan the ∧ column for its single T — both inputs must be true.
easy.explanation: Conjunction is true only in the T/T row; every row with a false input is false.
easy.deepDive: The ∧ table is T only at (T,T) and F elsewhere. This single-true-row pattern is the mirror of ∨, which is F only at (F,F). Memorizing '∧ needs all, ∨ needs one' prevents swapping them. Mixed rows always falsify ∧.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One false conjunct sinks a conjunction — this row is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One false conjunct sinks a conjunction — this row is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two false conjuncts give false, not true.

easy.prompt: In which row is P ∨ Q false?
easy.hint: Next step: look for the row where NOTHING is true — ∨ fails only there.
easy.explanation: Disjunction is false only when both disjuncts are false; any true input makes it true.
easy.deepDive: The ∨ table is F only at (F,F) and T in the other three rows. Inclusive 'or' asks 'is at least one true?' — with none true the answer is no. Mixed rows satisfy it. Confusing ∨ with ∧ would pick (T,T) as the only true row, which is wrong.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One true disjunct suffices, so this mixed row is true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One true disjunct suffices, so this mixed row is true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two true disjuncts certainly make inclusive 'or' true.

easy.prompt: P is true and Q is true. In the truth table, what is the value of ¬(P ∧ Q)?

choices.label: C
choices.body: True, because one negation flips the whole row

easy.hint: Next step: evaluate inside-out — first P ∧ Q, then apply the outer ¬.
easy.explanation: P ∧ Q is T∧T = true, and negating gives false.
easy.deepDive: Parentheses force the ∧ first: T∧T = T. The outer ¬ then flips T to F. Errors come from distributing ¬ incorrectly (treating it as preserving) or flipping before finishing the ∧. Inside-out evaluation — inner connective, then outer — always works.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Negation reverses rather than preserves — ¬(T∧T) is ¬T = F.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The flip happens after the ∧ is computed, giving ¬T = F, not T.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: All inputs are valued, so the compound has a definite value: false.

easy.prompt: The truth table for P → Q is false in exactly which row?
easy.hint: Next step: find the broken promise — true antecedent, false consequent.
easy.explanation: Material implication fails only on T→F; the other three rows are true.
easy.deepDive: Read P → Q as the promise 'if P then Q'. Genuine keeping (T→T) is true, and both untriggered cases (F→T, F→F) are vacuously true. Only triggering the antecedent while failing the consequent breaks it. Hence exactly one false row out of four.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A false antecedent makes the implication vacuously true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A false antecedent makes the implication vacuously true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A kept promise (true antecedent, true consequent) is true.

easy.prompt: Which row makes P → Q true while P is false?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both F→T and F→F rows (any Q works)

choices.label: D
choices.body: No row with P false is true

easy.hint: Next step: fix P = F and vary Q — check each of the two rows.
easy.explanation: With P false, both Q = true and Q = false give a true implication (vacuous truth).
easy.deepDive: Vacuous truth covers both false-antecedent rows: F→T and F→F are both T. So a false P guarantees truth regardless of Q. Picking only one row halves the pattern. Claiming none are true repeats the 'F→anything is F' misconception — the opposite of the truth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: F→F is also true — vacuous truth does not depend on Q.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: F→T is also true — vacuous truth does not depend on Q.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both false-antecedent rows are true; that is exactly vacuous truth.

easy.prompt: How many rows of the P → Q table are true?
easy.hint: Next step: count every row except the single T→F falsifier.
easy.explanation: Three rows are true (T→T, F→T, F→F); only T→F is false.
easy.deepDive: The → table is 75% true: T→T genuine, F→T and F→F vacuous. Only T→F fails. Contrast ∧ (one true row) and ↔ (two true rows). Counting 1 confuses → with ∧; counting 2 confuses it with ↔; counting 4 mistakes it for a tautology.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the true-row count for ∧, not →.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is the true-row count for ↔, not →.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: T→F is false, so → is not a tautology.

easy.prompt: An argument is valid if and only if…

choices.label: A
choices.body: It is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false.

easy.hint: Next step: focus on the LINK — validity asks whether true premises would GUARANTEE a true conclusion.
easy.explanation: Validity is truth-preservation: no situation with true premises and a false conclusion.
easy.deepDive: Validity is a property of the argument's form, not of actual truth. A valid argument with false premises can still conclude falsely. Premise truth (option B) plus validity gives soundness. Conclusion truth alone (option C) can arise from invalid reasoning. Persuasiveness is rhetoric, not logic.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: True premises plus validity is soundness — validity alone allows false premises.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A true conclusion can come from invalid reasoning with false premises.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Length and persuasiveness are rhetorical, not logical, properties.

easy.prompt: Which argument is VALID?

choices.label: A
choices.body: "All cats are mammals; Whiskers is a cat; so Whiskers is a mammal."

choices.label: B
choices.body: "Whiskers is a mammal; so Whiskers is a cat."

choices.label: C
choices.body: "Whiskers is a cat; so Whiskers likes tuna."

choices.label: D
choices.body: "Some cats are mammals; Whiskers is a cat; so Whiskers is a mammal."

easy.hint: Next step: test whether true premises could still leave the conclusion false — only one option survives.
easy.explanation: Universal premise plus membership forces the conclusion in every situation.
easy.deepDive: Option A is Barbara-style: every cat is a mammal, so any cat (Whiskers) must be one. Option B affirms the consequent (dogs are mammals too). Option C adds unrelated tuna content. Option D's 'some' premise leaves room for Whiskers to be a non-mammal cat. Validity means no counter-situation exists.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Mammals include dogs — Whiskers could be a dog, so premises could hold with a false conclusion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Nothing links cats to tuna; the conclusion adds unsupported content.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 'Some' leaves open that Whiskers is one of the non-mammal cats.

easy.prompt: Can a valid argument have a false conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Yes — if at least one premise is false.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No — valid arguments always conclude truly.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No — validity requires all premises true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Yes — even with all premises true.

easy.hint: Next step: recall validity only bans ONE combination — true premises with a false conclusion.
easy.explanation: Validity permits false conclusions whenever a premise is false; it only forbids true-premises/false-conclusion.
easy.deepDive: Example: 'All birds are fish; Tweety is a bird; so Tweety is a fish' is valid in form with a false conclusion from a false premise. Option B confuses validity with soundness. Option C folds premise truth into validity. Option D is impossible — true premises in a valid argument guarantee a true conclusion.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes sound arguments; validity alone allows false premises.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Premise truth is soundness territory, not validity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: True premises in a valid argument always yield a true conclusion — that combination is banned.

easy.prompt: A sound argument is one that is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Valid and has all true premises.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Invalid but has a true conclusion.

easy.hint: Next step: combine the two requirements — good FORM plus true STARTING points.
easy.explanation: Soundness = validity + actually true premises, which guarantees a true conclusion.
easy.deepDive: Validity is form; premise truth is content; soundness needs both. A valid argument from false premises is unsound. An invalid argument is unsound even with true premises and conclusion. Persuasion is irrelevant — soundness is objective. Sound arguments are the gold standard: airtight reasoning from true starting points.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Validity alone allows false premises — that is merely valid, not sound.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Invalidity always means unsound, however true the conclusion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Persuasion is rhetoric; soundness is validity plus true premises.

easy.prompt: "All fish live in water; Nemo is a fish; so Nemo lives in water." If both premises are true, the argument is…
easy.hint: Next step: check form first (does the conclusion follow?), then premise truth.
easy.explanation: The form is valid and the premises are true, so both soundness conditions are met.
easy.deepDive: Form check: any fish (Nemo) must live in water given the universal — valid. Content check: both premises are true — sound. 'Valid but unsound' would need a false premise. 'Invalid but sound' is impossible, since soundness requires validity. Stepwise checking (form, then content) classifies every argument.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Unsoundness needs a false premise or invalid form — neither is present here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Soundness requires validity, so 'invalid but sound' can never occur.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The universal-plus-instance form guarantees validity.

easy.prompt: "All birds can fly; penguins are birds; so penguins can fly." The argument is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Valid but unsound (first premise is false).

easy.hint: Next step: separate form from content — does the conclusion follow, and is every premise true?
easy.explanation: The form is airtight but 'all birds can fly' is false (penguins, ostriches), so it is valid yet unsound.
easy.deepDive: Validity: any bird, penguin included, would fly IF the universal held — the link is good. Soundness: the universal is factually false, so the argument is unsound despite validity. This is the flagship valid-but-unsound case. Calling it sound ignores the false premise; calling it invalid ignores the good form.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Soundness needs all premises true — the first premise is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The universal-plus-instance form is valid; the flaw is content, not form.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Soundness requires validity, so this combination is impossible — and the form here is valid anyway.

easy.prompt: From P → Q and P, we may conclude Q. This rule is called…
easy.hint: Next step: affirming the ANTECEDENT (P) to get the consequent — which 'modus' does that?
easy.explanation: Modus ponens affirms the antecedent: P→Q plus P yields Q.
easy.deepDive: MP is implication-elimination: given the conditional and its antecedent, detach the consequent. Modus tollens instead denies the consequent (¬Q) to get ¬P. Disjunctive syllogism works on ∨ with a denial. Conjunction introduction builds ∧ rather than eliminating →. Name by what is affirmed or denied.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Modus tollens needs ¬Q (denying the consequent), not P.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Disjunctive syllogism uses P ∨ Q plus ¬P — no conditional here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That builds conjunctions; this eliminates an implication.

easy.prompt: From P → Q and ¬Q, we may conclude ¬P. This rule is called…
easy.hint: Next step: denying the CONSEQUENT (¬Q) to deny the antecedent — which rule is that?
easy.explanation: Modus tollens denies the consequent: P→Q plus ¬Q yields ¬P.
easy.deepDive: MT is the contrapositive in rule form: with Q ruled out, P cannot hold (else Q would). Modus ponens needs P, not ¬Q. Hypothetical syllogism chains two conditionals (P→Q, Q→R). Affirming the consequent (P→Q, Q ∴ P) is the fallacy MT is often confused with — note MT denies Q while the fallacy affirms it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Modus ponens affirms P; here Q is denied instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That chains P→Q with Q→R — only one conditional is present here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That fallacy affirms Q; here Q is denied (¬Q), making it valid.

easy.prompt: From P ∨ Q and ¬P, we may conclude Q. This rule is called…
easy.hint: Next step: one disjunct denied, the other asserted — which ∨-rule is that?
easy.explanation: Disjunctive syllogism: with P ruled out, the ∨ forces Q.
easy.deepDive: A true disjunction needs at least one true side; ¬P eliminates the first, leaving Q. MP and MT work on conditionals, not disjunctions. Denying the antecedent is an invalid →-pattern (P→Q, ¬P ∴ ¬Q). Classifying by the main connective (∨ vs →) picks the right rule.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Modus ponens needs a conditional P → Q, not a disjunction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Modus tollens needs a conditional plus ¬Q, not P ∨ Q plus ¬P.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is an invalid →-pattern; this ∨-inference is valid.

easy.prompt: In first-order logic, ∀x F(x) means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every element of the domain has property F.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exactly one element has property F.

easy.hint: Next step: expand ∀ as 'for every' — how many domain elements must satisfy F?
easy.explanation: Universal quantification asserts F holds of all domain elements without exception.
easy.deepDive: ∀x F(x) is true iff every assignment to x satisfies F. One failure falsifies it. 'Some' is ∃, 'exactly one' is ∃!, 'none' is ¬∃ (or ∀¬). The domain fixes the range: 'every' means every member of the specified domain, nothing more.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is ∃x F(x) — one witness suffices, far weaker than ∀.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is ∃!x F(x) — uniqueness plus existence, not universality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is ¬∃x F(x) — the opposite extreme.

easy.prompt: "Every raven is black" with domain birds (R(x): x is a raven, B(x): x is black). Best symbolization?
easy.hint: Next step: restrict with → — the claim constrains ravens, not every bird.
easy.explanation: Each bird: IF it is a raven THEN it is black; non-ravens satisfy vacuously.
easy.deepDive: Universals restrict via →: non-ravens make R(x) false so R(x)→B(x) is vacuously true, exactly as 'every raven' intends. ∧ would demand every bird be a black raven — far stronger. ∃ weakens to 'some bird'. Swapping to B→R claims all black birds are ravens (the converse error).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That says every bird is a black raven — non-ravens would falsify it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That says some bird satisfies the conditional — far weaker than 'every'.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is the converse: all black birds are ravens — false (crows).

easy.prompt: ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) is false exactly when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Some element satisfies P but not Q.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Some element satisfies neither P nor Q.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every element satisfies both P and Q.

easy.hint: Next step: hunt for the row that falsifies →, lifted to an element.
easy.explanation: A universal fails via one counterexample: an element with P true and Q false.
easy.deepDive: ∀x(R(x)) fails iff ∃x(¬R(x)); here R(x) is P(x)→Q(x), whose negation is P(x)∧¬Q(x). So falsity needs a P-non-Q witness. Neither-neither elements satisfy the conditional vacuously (F→F). All-both confirms. Empty P-extension makes it vacuously true. One witness kills; zero witnesses can only confirm instances.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Neither-neither gives F→F = true — compatible with, not fatal to, the universal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That confirms the universal (every instance T→T), the opposite of falsifying.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Empty P makes every instance vacuously true — the universal holds.

easy.prompt: In first-order logic, ∃x F(x) means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: At least one element of the domain has property F.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every element of the domain has property F.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No element of the domain has property F.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exactly one element has property F.

easy.hint: Next step: expand ∃ as 'there exists' — how many witnesses are needed?
easy.explanation: Existential quantification needs just one witness satisfying F.
easy.deepDive: ∃x F(x) is true iff some assignment satisfies F; one witness suffices, more are fine. ∀ demands all. ¬∃ (none) is the opposite. Exactly-one (∃!) adds uniqueness — stronger than ∃. So ∃ is the weakest positive claim: 'at least one'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is ∀x F(x) — all elements, far stronger than one witness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is ¬∃x F(x) — the negation of the existential.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is ∃!x F(x) — existence plus uniqueness, stronger than ∃.

easy.prompt: "Some prime is even" (P(x): x is prime, E(x): x is even). Best symbolization?
easy.hint: Next step: demand a witness with BOTH traits — existentials restrict with ∧, not →.
easy.explanation: Need an x that is prime AND even (namely 2); → would be satisfied by any non-prime.
easy.deepDive: Existentials restrict via ∧: the witness must satisfy both properties. With →, any non-prime (e.g., 9: F→anything = T) would 'witness' the claim — even if no even prime existed. ∀ versions claim about all numbers. The ∧/→ swap (∀↔→, ∃↔∧) is the most-tested translation rule in predicate logic.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Any non-prime (e.g., 9) makes P→E vacuously true — witness would prove nothing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That says every number is an even prime — wildly false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That says all primes are even — false (3, 5, 7, …).

easy.prompt: ∃x (P(x) → Q(x)) is troublesome as a translation of 'some P is Q' because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Any non-P element already makes it true, even with no P-that-is-Q.

easy.hint: Next step: test a non-P element in P(x) → Q(x) — what row do you get?
easy.explanation: Non-P elements give F→anything = true, so the existential is satisfied spuriously.
easy.deepDive: If anything is non-P (say a rock when P = raven), then P(rock)→Q(rock) is F→… = T, witnessing ∃x(P(x)→Q(x)) with no genuine P-that-is-Q. So the formula is nearly trivially true whenever non-Ps exist. Genuine 'some P is Q' needs P(x)∧Q(x) — a witness with both. Conditionals under quantifiers are legal; they are just the wrong restrictor for ∃.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: It is nearly trivially true (not contradictory) whenever a non-P exists.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: It is true too easily — non-P witnesses abound.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Conditionals nest under quantifiers freely; the issue is meaning, not syntax.

easy.prompt: In ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)), the variable x is…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Free in P(x) but bound in Q(x).

easy.hint: Next step: check whether x sits inside the quantifier's parentheses — if so it is bound.
easy.explanation: Both occurrences of x lie within ∀x's scope, so both are bound.
easy.deepDive: Scope = the formula the quantifier governs (here P(x)→Q(x)). Every x inside is bound — boundness is positional, not split across connectives. Free variables stand outside all governing quantifiers. Constants are separate symbols (a, b, c), not variables. Since no free x remains, the whole formula is a sentence with a truth value per model.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Free means outside every governing quantifier — x here is inside ∀x's scope.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Scope covers the whole conditional, not one side — both occurrences are bound.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: x is a variable bound by a quantifier, not a constant symbol.

easy.prompt: In (∀x P(x)) ∨ Q(x), the LAST occurrence of x (in Q(x)) is…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Bound by the ∀x on the left.

easy.hint: Next step: bracket the ∀x's scope — does it extend past the ∨?
easy.explanation: ∀x governs only P(x) in the left disjunct; the x in Q(x) is outside, hence free.
easy.deepDive: Quantifier scope ends where its parentheses close: (∀x P(x)) is a closed unit, and ∨ joins it with open Q(x). So the formula has bound x (left) and free x (right) — same letter, different roles. ∨ binds nothing; only quantifiers bind. Such mixed formulas are open (not sentences) because a free variable remains.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The left ∀x's scope closed before the ∨ — it cannot reach Q(x).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Connectives never bind variables; only ∀ and ∃ do.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One OCCURRENCE is one or the other — this occurrence is free (an earlier one is bound).

easy.prompt: Which formula is a sentence (no free variables)?
easy.hint: Next step: check each variable — is every occurrence inside some quantifier's scope?
easy.explanation: x is bound by ∀x and y by ∃y; the rest leave variables free.
easy.deepDive: Sentences (closed formulas) get truth values in models; open formulas need assignments too. In ∀x∃yR(x,y), ∀x covers x's spot and ∃y covers y's — nothing dangles. ∀xR(x,y) leaves y free. P(x)→Q(x) leaves both x's free. The last option binds nothing. Only sentences express complete claims.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: y never falls under a quantifier — free, so the formula is open.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: No quantifiers at all — both x's are free.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: No quantifiers bind x, y, or z — all free.

medium.prompt: The implication P → Q is false in exactly which case?
medium.hint: Next step: look for the broken promise — a true antecedent with a false consequent.
medium.explanation: Material implication is false only when a true P leads to a false Q; all other rows are true.
medium.deepDive: Think of P → Q as the promise 'if P then Q'. Only a kept-antecedent with a failed consequent breaks it. Rows with P false keep the promise vacuously. The T→T row keeps it genuinely. Hence exactly one false row: T→F.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: With P false the implication is vacuously true, not false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: With P false the implication is vacuously true, not false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A true antecedent delivering a true consequent keeps the promise — true.

medium.prompt: Let P be false and Q be false. What is the truth value of P → Q?

choices.label: B
choices.body: False, because false cannot imply false

choices.label: C
choices.body: False, because the antecedent is false

medium.hint: Next step: ask whether P is true — if not, the implication is already vacuously true.
medium.explanation: A false antecedent makes the implication vacuously true, so F → F is true.
medium.deepDive: Material → cares only about the T→F counterexample. When P is false, no counterexample is possible, so the implication defaults to true. This vacuous truth surprises newcomers who expect 'false implies false' to fail. But logic treats untriggered conditionals as kept promises.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This treats → like a causal story; materially, F → F has no counterexample so it is true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A false antecedent is exactly what makes an implication vacuously true, not false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Every truth-valued P and Q give → a definite value — here true.

medium.prompt: "If the moon is made of cheese, then 2 + 2 = 4." As a material implication, it is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: True, because the antecedent is false

choices.label: B
choices.body: False, because the antecedent is silly

choices.label: C
choices.body: False, because cheese has nothing to do with arithmetic

choices.label: D
choices.body: Neither, since the antecedent is absurd

medium.hint: Next step: check the antecedent's truth value before worrying about relevance.
medium.explanation: The moon is not made of cheese, so the antecedent is false and the material conditional is vacuously true.
medium.deepDive: Material implication ignores relevance and causation; only truth values matter. A false antecedent yields truth regardless of topic connection. This is why 'if 0 = 1 then anything' is true in mathematics. Relevance logics add extra constraints, but classical → does not.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Silliness does not falsify →; only a true antecedent with false consequent does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Classical → tracks truth values, not topic relevance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Absurd-but-false antecedents still give a truth value: vacuously true.

medium.prompt: Let P be false and Q be true. What is P → Q?

choices.label: B
choices.body: False, because a false P cannot imply anything

choices.label: C
choices.body: False, because P and Q differ

choices.label: D
choices.body: True only if Q caused P

medium.hint: Next step: scan for the one falsifying pattern T→F — is it present here?
medium.explanation: F → T is not the falsifying T → F pattern, so the implication is true.
medium.deepDive: The → table: T→T true, T→F false, F→T true, F→F true. Both false-antecedent rows are true. Differing values do not falsify; only true-antecedent plus false-consequent does. Causation is irrelevant to the material reading.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: False antecedents imply everything vacuously — that is the opposite of the error.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Difference of values is the biconditional's concern, not implication's.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Material → needs no causal link, only the absence of T→F.

medium.prompt: The converse of P → Q is…
medium.hint: Next step: swap the two sides without adding any negations.
medium.explanation: The converse swaps antecedent and consequent, giving Q → P.
medium.deepDive: From P → Q, three lookalikes arise: converse Q → P (swap), inverse ¬P → ¬Q (negate both), contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P (swap and negate). Only the contrapositive is equivalent to the original. Swapping alone changes meaning, as 'if it rains the street is wet' versus 'if the street is wet it rains' shows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That swaps AND negates — it is the contrapositive, not the converse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That negates both sides without swapping — it is the inverse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That negates only the consequent, which is none of the three forms.

medium.prompt: The contrapositive of P → Q is…
medium.hint: Next step: swap the sides AND negate both — that is the two-move version.
medium.explanation: Contraposition swaps and negates, giving ¬Q → ¬P, which is equivalent to P → Q.
medium.deepDive: Contrapositive is the only equivalent rephrasing of an implication. Its table matches P → Q row for row, since both fail exactly on P-true-Q-false. Converse and inverse match each other instead. So proving the contrapositive proves the original.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That swaps only — the converse, not equivalent in general.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That negates only — the inverse, not equivalent in general.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That negates the antecedent and swaps incorrectly; not a standard form.

medium.prompt: "If you live in Calgary, then you live in Alberta." Which is its contrapositive?

choices.label: A
choices.body: "If you do not live in Alberta, then you do not live in Calgary."

choices.label: B
choices.body: "If you live in Alberta, then you live in Calgary."

choices.label: C
choices.body: "If you do not live in Calgary, then you do not live in Alberta."

choices.label: D
choices.body: "If you live in Calgary, then you do not live in Alberta."

medium.hint: Next step: start from 'not in Alberta' — what must follow about Calgary?
medium.explanation: Contraposition gives 'not in Alberta → not in Calgary', which is equivalent to the original.
medium.deepDive: Living in Calgary entails living in Alberta, so failing the consequent (outside Alberta) forces failing the antecedent (outside Calgary). The converse would wrongly claim all Albertans live in Calgary. The inverse makes the same error negatively. Only the contrapositive preserves truth.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the converse — false, since Edmonton is in Alberta but not Calgary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is the inverse — also false for the same Edmonton reason.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That contradicts the original instead of rephrasing it.

medium.prompt: Original: "If it is a dog, then it is a mammal." Which rephrasing is logically equivalent?

choices.label: A
choices.body: "If it is not a mammal, then it is not a dog."

choices.label: B
choices.body: "If it is a mammal, then it is a dog."

choices.label: C
choices.body: "If it is not a dog, then it is not a mammal."

choices.label: D
choices.body: "It is a dog if and only if it is a mammal."

medium.hint: Next step: pick the option that both swaps and negates — cats will test the others.
medium.explanation: The contrapositive 'non-mammal → non-dog' is equivalent; converse and inverse fail because cats are mammals but not dogs.
medium.deepDive: A cat is a non-dog mammal, which refutes both converse (mammal → dog) and inverse (non-dog → non-mammal). No counterexample touches the contrapositive, since anything that is not a mammal cannot be a dog. Equivalence means sharing all counterexamples — only the contrapositive does.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The converse is refuted by a cat: a mammal that is not a dog.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The inverse is refuted by a cat: not a dog yet still a mammal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The biconditional adds the false converse direction, so it is strictly stronger.

medium.prompt: "If it rains, then the street is wet" is true. What follows?

choices.label: A
choices.body: "If the street is dry, then it is not raining."

choices.label: B
choices.body: "If the street is wet, then it is raining."

choices.label: C
choices.body: "If it does not rain, then the street is dry."

choices.label: D
choices.body: "It is raining and the street is dry."

medium.hint: Next step: use the contrapositive — a dry street rules out rain.
medium.explanation: Only the contrapositive follows; wet streets can come from sprinklers, and dry non-rainy days are compatible with the original.
medium.deepDive: Implication forbids exactly one situation: rain without wetness. A sprinkler gives wetness without rain, refuting the converse. A sunny day gives no rain and dryness, consistent with the original but not proving the inverse. The contrapositive restates the same forbidden combination from the other side.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: This is the converse — a sprinkler can wet the street with no rain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: This is the inverse — sprinklers again allow wet streets without rain.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is precisely the one combination the true implication rules out.

medium.prompt: Which English sentence is best symbolized as P → Q (P: "you study", Q: "you pass")?

choices.label: C
choices.body: "You study if and only if you pass."

medium.hint: Next step: look for the 'if … then …' structure with study as the condition.
medium.explanation: "If you study, then you pass" puts studying as antecedent and passing as consequent, matching P → Q.
medium.deepDive: 'And' is a conjunction P ∧ Q, strictly stronger than the conditional. 'If and only if' is the biconditional P ↔ Q, asserting both directions. 'Pass, therefore studied' argues Q → P (the converse). Only 'if study then pass' captures the single direction P → Q.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That asserts both happened — a conjunction, not a conditional.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That asserts both directions — a biconditional, stronger than P → Q.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That infers the antecedent from the consequent — the converse direction.

medium.prompt: "P only if Q" is best symbolized as…
medium.hint: Next step: rephrase as 'if P is true, Q must be true' and match the arrow.
medium.explanation: "P only if Q" means P cannot be true without Q, i.e., P → Q.
medium.deepDive: 'Only if' sets a necessary condition: P requires Q. So P-true forces Q-true, exactly the T→F ban of P → Q. By contrast 'P if Q' gives Q → P (Q suffices for P). Confusing the two swaps antecedent and consequent — the classic converse error in translation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is 'P if Q' (Q suffices for P) — the reverse direction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That asserts both P and Q outright instead of a conditional link.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That asserts both 'P only if Q' and 'P if Q' together — too strong.

medium.prompt: "You can ride unless you are under 12" (R: ride, U: under 12). Best symbolization?
medium.hint: Next step: rephrase 'unless' as 'if not … then …' with 'not under 12' first.
medium.explanation: "Unless" means 'if not': not-under-12 implies ride, i.e., ¬U → R.
medium.deepDive: 'A unless B' standardly means 'if not B then A', equivalently 'A or B'. Here being 12+ suffices for riding. U → R would wrongly let under-12s ride. R → U would wrongly require riders to be under 12. The conjunction describes one scenario, not the rule.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That says being under 12 gets you a ride — the opposite of the rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That says riders must be under 12 — backwards.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes one forbidden case, not the whole conditional rule.

medium.prompt: Which is logically equivalent to ¬(P ∧ Q)?
medium.hint: Next step: push the ¬ inward — flip ∧ to ∨ and negate each side.
medium.explanation: De Morgan's law: negating a conjunction gives the disjunction of the negations.
medium.deepDive: Check row T∧T: ¬(T∧T) = F, and ¬T∨¬T = F∨F = F — match. In every other row P∧Q is already F so its negation is T, while at least one of ¬P, ¬Q is T, so the disjunction is T. Keeping ∧ unchanged (option B) is the classic De Morgan mistake — the connective must flip.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That keeps ∧ instead of flipping to ∨ — it is ¬(P ∨ Q), the other De Morgan law.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropping the negations changes every row; check T∧T where ¬(P∧Q) is F but P∨Q is T.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is true only in the single T/F row, not in all three rows where ¬(P∧Q) holds.

medium.prompt: Which is logically equivalent to ¬(P ∨ Q)?
medium.hint: Next step: push the ¬ inward — flip ∨ to ∧ and negate each side.
medium.explanation: De Morgan's law: negating a disjunction gives the conjunction of the negations.
medium.deepDive: ¬(P∨Q) is true only when P∨Q is false, i.e., only in row F/F — exactly where ¬P∧¬Q is T∧T = T. In every other row at least one of P, Q is true, so both ¬(P∨Q) and ¬P∧¬Q are false. Keeping ∨ (option B) is the mirror-image error: the connective must flip on every De Morgan push.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That keeps ∨ instead of flipping to ∧ — it is ¬(P ∧ Q), the other law.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dropping the negations inverts the table; check F/F where ¬(P∨Q) is T but P∧Q is F.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is P → Q, whose three true rows differ from the single true row here.

medium.prompt: "It is not the case that Pia is both tired and hungry" (T ∧ H). Equivalent claim?

choices.label: A
choices.body: "Pia is not tired, or Pia is not hungry (or both)."

choices.label: D
choices.body: "If Pia is tired then she is hungry."

medium.hint: Next step: one missing condition suffices — translate 'not both' as an 'or' of absences.
medium.explanation: ¬(T∧H) ≡ ¬T ∨ ¬H: at least one of tiredness, hunger is absent.
medium.deepDive: Denying 'both' is weak: Pia could be tired-but-fed, hungry-but-rested, or neither — three scenarios, matching the three true rows of the disjunction. 'Neither' allows only the last scenario (one row), so it is strictly stronger. Plain 'tired or hungry' asserts presence rather than absence. The conditional says something narrower still.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is ¬T ∧ ¬H (neither) — true in only one row, stronger than 'not both'.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That drops the negations, asserting presence instead of absence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is T → H, true in three rows but a different three-row pattern of commitment.

medium.prompt: "The switch is not (up or on)" — ¬(U ∨ O). Equivalent claim?

choices.label: A
choices.body: "The switch is not up and not on."

choices.label: B
choices.body: "The switch is not up or not on."

choices.label: D
choices.body: "If it is up then it is on."

medium.hint: Next step: denying an 'or' denies EACH option — join the denials with 'and'.
medium.explanation: ¬(U∨O) ≡ ¬U ∧ ¬O: both disjuncts fail.
medium.deepDive: A disjunction is easy to satisfy (one true suffices) so denying it is strong: both must fail. Hence the single true row F/F, matching ¬U∧¬O. The 'or' of denials (option B) is the weak 'not both' claim with three true rows. Dropping negations or switching to a conditional describes unrelated patterns.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is ¬(U ∧ O) — the weak 'not both', true in three rows, not one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That drops the negation entirely, asserting the opposite.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is U → O, a different three-true-row pattern.

medium.prompt: Which is logically equivalent to ¬(P → Q)?
medium.hint: Next step: ask which single row falsifies P → Q, then describe that row as a conjunction.
medium.explanation: P → Q fails only on T→F, and P ∧ ¬Q is true exactly there.
medium.deepDive: Negating a conditional asserts the forbidden combination: antecedent true, consequent false. So ¬(P→Q) has one true row (T/F), matching P∧¬Q. Option C (¬P∨Q) is P→Q itself. Option B (¬P→¬Q, the inverse) has three true rows. Option D needs both false — a different single row.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The inverse ¬P → ¬Q has three true rows; the negation of → has just one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ¬P ∨ Q is P → Q itself, the opposite of its negation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ¬P ∧ ¬Q is true only in row F/F, but ¬(P→Q) is true only in row T/F.

medium.prompt: "It is false that if it rains then the game is cancelled" — ¬(R → C). What actually happened?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It rained and the game was NOT cancelled.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It did not rain and the game was not cancelled.

choices.label: C
choices.body: If it did not rain then the game was not cancelled.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It did not rain or the game was cancelled.

medium.hint: Next step: denying 'if R then C' produces the one counterexample — rain without cancellation.
medium.explanation: ¬(R→C) ≡ R ∧ ¬C: the antecedent held and the consequent failed.
medium.deepDive: A conditional is refuted by exhibiting its forbidden row: true antecedent with false consequent. Here that means rain fell yet the game went on. Dry weather with no cancellation (option B) actually confirms the conditional vacuously. Options C and D restate the inverse and the original conditional respectively — both compatible with, not denials of, R→C.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No rain makes R → C vacuously true, so this confirms rather than denies it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is the inverse ¬R → ¬C — compatible with R → C, not its denial.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is ¬R ∨ C, i.e., R → C itself — the opposite of its negation.

medium.prompt: P → Q is logically equivalent to which of the following?
medium.hint: Next step: match the three true rows — rule out the consequent-false row with ¬Q, or the antecedent-true row with ¬P.
medium.explanation: ¬P ∨ Q is false only when ¬P is false and Q is false, i.e., exactly the T→F row.
medium.deepDive: Both P→Q and ¬P∨Q fail in exactly one row: P true with Q false. In all other rows at least one of ¬P, Q is true. Conjunction P∧Q is far stricter (one true row). ¬P∧¬Q needs both false (one, different row). P∨¬Q fails on F→T instead — the mirror image.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: P ∧ Q is true in only one row; the implication is true in three.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ¬P ∧ ¬Q is true only in row F/F; the implication is true in three rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P ∨ ¬Q is false in row F/T — it is Q → P (the converse), not P → Q.

medium.prompt: Which formula is the negation of P → Q (i.e., equivalent to ¬(P → Q))?
medium.hint: Next step: eliminate the options that have three true rows — the negation has only one.
medium.explanation: Only P ∧ ¬Q has the single true row T/F matching ¬(P→Q).
medium.deepDive: Count true rows: P∧¬Q has one (T/F); ¬P∨¬Q has three (all but T/T); Q→P has three (all but F→T... precisely rows where Q-true-or-P-false fails only at F/T); ¬P∨Q has three (all but T/F). The negated conditional's single true row T/F matches only the conjunction. Row-counting is a fast equivalence filter.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Three true rows — that is ¬(P ∧ Q), not ¬(P → Q).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Three true rows — the converse, not the negation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Three true rows — that is P → Q itself.

medium.prompt: Which formula is a tautology?
medium.hint: Next step: test both rows P = T and P = F — which formula stays true in each?
medium.explanation: P ∨ ¬P is true whether P is true or false (excluded middle); the rest fail in at least one row.
medium.deepDive: A tautology is true in every row. P∨¬P: if P is T the first disjunct holds; if P is F the second holds. P∧¬P is the mirror contradiction, false in both rows. P∧P just repeats P (contingent). Order of conjuncts never matters, so ¬P∧P is the same contradiction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a contradiction — false in both rows, the opposite of a tautology.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That repeats P, so it is true in one row and false in the other (contingent).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Conjunct order is irrelevant — this is the same contradiction as P ∧ ¬P.

medium.prompt: Which formula is a contradiction?
medium.hint: Next step: look for the formula false in BOTH rows — nothing can be true and false at once.
medium.explanation: P ∧ ¬P demands P both true and false, impossible in every row.
medium.deepDive: A contradiction is false in every row. P∧¬P needs T∧F-structure in each row: with P true it is T∧F = F; with P false it is F∧T = F. The other options are all tautologies: P∨¬P and ¬P∨P (disjunct order irrelevant) cover both rows, and P→P never hits T→F.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the excluded-middle tautology — true in both rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: P → P never instantiates T→F, so it is true in both rows (tautology).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Disjunct order does not matter — this is the same tautology as P ∨ ¬P.

medium.prompt: Which formula is contingent (true in some rows, false in others)?
medium.hint: Next step: find the formula whose table mixes T and F — count its true rows.
medium.explanation: P → Q is true in three rows but false in T→F, so it is contingent.
medium.deepDive: Contingent means mixed: at least one true row and at least one false row. P→Q qualifies (3T/1F). P∨¬P is all-true (tautology). Q∧¬Q is all-false (contradiction). A disjunction of two contradictions is still all-false — F∨F = F in every row — so option D is a contradiction, not contingent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: All-true in every row — a tautology, not contingent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: All-false in every row — a contradiction, not contingent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: F∨F in every row stays all-false — a (compound) contradiction.

medium.prompt: P ∨ ¬P is a tautology and P ∧ ¬P is a contradiction. What is P → ¬P?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Contingent (true when P false, false when P true)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Tautology, since every implication with ¬ is one

choices.label: C
choices.body: Contradiction, since it contains P and ¬P

medium.hint: Next step: evaluate both rows — P = T gives T→F, P = F gives F→T.
medium.explanation: P → ¬P is F in row T and T in row F, so it mixes values: contingent.
medium.deepDive: Not every formula containing P and ¬P is extreme: the connective decides. T→F = F but F→T = T, hence mixed. Equivalently P→¬P ≡ ¬P∨¬P ≡ ¬P, which plainly varies with P. 'Contains ¬ so tautology' and 'contains both so contradiction' are pattern-matching errors — only the full table classifies.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Row P = T gives T→F = F, so it is not all-true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Row P = F gives F→T = T, so it is not all-false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P ∨ ¬P is all-true; P → ¬P is false in row T — different tables.

medium.prompt: "If it rains (R), the street is wet (W). It is raining." What validly follows by modus ponens?
medium.hint: Next step: match R → W with asserted R — detach the consequent.
medium.explanation: MP: R→W plus R detaches W.
medium.deepDive: Modus ponens fires when the conditional's antecedent is affirmed. Here R is given, so W follows in one step. 'Dry' would need ¬W machinery. 'Not raining' contradicts the given. 'Nothing follows' misses the textbook MP setup — conditional plus antecedent always detaches.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the opposite of the detached consequent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That contradicts the given premise that it is raining.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Conditional plus antecedent always yields the consequent by MP.

medium.prompt: "If you study (S), you pass (P). You studied." A classmate concludes you might still fail. Why is that wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Modus ponens guarantees P: S→P with S asserted forces P.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It affirms the consequent, which is valid.

medium.hint: Next step: check whether the valid MP conclusion was dodged — S and S→P leave no room for ¬P.
medium.explanation: Given S→P and S, ¬P would make the premises true with a false conclusion — impossible, so P follows.
medium.deepDive: MP's guarantee is semantic: the only S→P row with S true is T→T, i.e., P true. 'Might fail' claims row T→F is live, but that row falsifies S→P. Affirming the consequent (option B) is a different, invalid pattern. The contrapositive is valid but unneeded — MP fires directly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That pattern (S→P, P ∴ S) is invalid and is not what happened here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The conditional S→P explicitly links studying to passing.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The contrapositive is valid but MP already fires directly on S.

medium.prompt: Given A → B, B → C, and A, which chain reaches C?

choices.label: A
choices.body: MP on A→B gives B; MP on B→C gives C.

choices.label: B
choices.body: MT on A→B gives ¬A; MP gives C.

medium.hint: Next step: fire MP on the first conditional, then reuse its output on the second.
medium.explanation: Two MP steps chain the implications: A yields B, B yields C.
medium.deepDive: Step 1: A→B with A detaches B. Step 2: B→C with freshly-derived B detaches C. This is hypothetical syllogism (A→C) plus MP, done stepwise. MT needs denials, which are absent. Jumping A∴C skips the licensed steps. Denying B would give ¬A via MT — the wrong direction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MT needs ¬B, which is not given — and ¬A would block, not reach, C.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: C needs the two licensed MP steps; jumping is not a rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Denying B gives ¬A (MT), moving away from C.

medium.prompt: "If the alarm works (A), it rings (R). It is not ringing." What validly follows by modus tollens?
medium.hint: Next step: match A → R with denied consequent ¬R — deny the antecedent side.
medium.explanation: MT: A→R plus ¬R yields ¬A.
medium.deepDive: With R false, A-true would make the forbidden T→F row, so A must be false. That is modus tollens, the contrapositive as a rule. Affirming A would contradict ¬R. Reasserting R contradicts the given. 'Nothing follows' misses the textbook MT setup — conditional plus denied consequent always detaches ¬A.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A-true with R-false is the forbidden T→F row — ruled out.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That contradicts the given ¬R.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Conditional plus denied consequent always yields ¬A by MT.

medium.prompt: "If the file saved (S), the icon changes (I). The icon did not change." A user concludes the file saved anyway. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: MT forces ¬S: S→I with ¬I rules out S.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The icon is irrelevant to saving.

medium.hint: Next step: suppose S were true with I false — does S→I survive?
medium.explanation: S-true with I-false falsifies S→I, so S must be false: the file did not save.
medium.deepDive: MT's semantic force: given ¬I, the only S→I-compatible row is F→F, i.e., ¬S. Concluding S claims the T→F row while keeping S→I — impossible. MP needs S affirmed, but S is what is at issue. The icon is the consequent, hence decisive when denied. Affirming the consequent (¬I is denying, not affirming) is the wrong rule.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MP needs the antecedent S affirmed; here the consequent is denied instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The conditional S→I explicitly links saving to the icon.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ¬I denies the consequent; affirming would need I asserted.

medium.prompt: Given P → Q and ¬Q, plus Q ∨ R, what follows?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ¬P by MT, then R by disjunctive syllogism.

medium.hint: Next step: first use ¬Q on the conditional, then feed the result into the disjunction.
medium.explanation: MT gives ¬P; that step is independent — and ¬Q with Q∨R gives R by disjunctive syllogism.
medium.deepDive: Step 1 (MT): P→Q plus ¬Q detaches ¬P. Step 2 (DS): Q∨R plus ¬Q forces R, since the first disjunct is dead. Both steps reuse ¬Q on different premises. MP needs P affirmed — absent. Affirming Q contradicts ¬Q. Multi-step proofs chain single rules, each licensed by its own premises.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MP needs P affirmed, but ¬Q plus P→Q gives ¬P instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Q is denied (¬Q given); affirming it contradicts a premise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Two licensed steps fire: MT on the conditional, DS on the disjunction.

medium.prompt: Affirming the consequent is the invalid pattern:

choices.label: A
choices.body: From P → Q and Q, infer P.

choices.label: B
choices.body: From P → Q and P, infer Q.

choices.label: D
choices.body: From P ∨ Q and ¬P, infer Q.

medium.hint: Next step: look for the pattern that treats the converse as proven — consequent affirmed, antecedent concluded.
medium.explanation: Q can hold without P (row F→T), so P→Q plus Q does not pin P.
medium.deepDive: The F→T row (sprinkler: no rain, wet street) keeps P→Q true with Q true and P false — a direct counterexample. Option B is modus ponens (valid). Option C is modus tollens (valid). Option D is disjunctive syllogism (valid). Only affirming the consequent mistakes Q-true for P-true.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is modus ponens — valid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is modus tollens — valid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is disjunctive syllogism — valid.

medium.prompt: Denying the antecedent is the invalid pattern:

choices.label: C
choices.body: From P → Q and P, infer Q.

medium.hint: Next step: look for ¬P used to kill Q — which rows with P false keep P→Q true?
medium.explanation: Both F→T and F→F keep P→Q true, so ¬P leaves Q unconstrained.
medium.deepDive: Denying the antecedent overclaims from vacuous truth: with P false, Q floats (sprinkler gives F→T; dry day gives F→F). So ¬Q is not forced. Option B is MT (valid). Option C is MP (valid). Option D is MP on a different conditional (valid) — denying nothing, just firing ¬P→¬Q with ¬P affirmed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is modus tollens — valid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is modus ponens — valid.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is modus ponens on ¬P → ¬Q — valid.

medium.prompt: "If you are a senior (S), you get a discount (D). Maya is not a senior." A cashier concludes Maya gets no discount. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Denying the antecedent — students or coupons could still give D.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Affirming the consequent — D was never affirmed.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Modus tollens was misapplied — ¬S is not ¬D.

medium.hint: Next step: ask whether D can hold without S — is the senior discount the only one?
medium.explanation: S→D with ¬S leaves D open (F→T row: non-senior with a student discount).
medium.deepDive: The counterexample is a non-senior with a discount via another route (student, coupon). That is row F→T: S false, D true, conditional intact. Affirming the consequent would need D affirmed — here S is denied instead. MT needs ¬D — absent. So the cashier denies the antecedent, the invalid ¬P ∴ ¬Q move.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nothing was affirmed here; S was denied, not D affirmed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: MT was not used at all — MT needs ¬D, which is absent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The F→T row (discounted non-senior) keeps premises true with a false conclusion.

medium.prompt: A student checks n = 3, 4, 5 for 'n² + n + 41 is prime' (all prime) and claims it holds for all n. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Examples are not a proof — one counterexample (n = 40) refutes it.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Three examples are too few; thirty would prove it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Primality cannot be checked for specific n.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Nothing — verifying cases 3–5 proves the universal.

medium.hint: Next step: recall universals need general reasons — can any finite sample rule out a later failure?
medium.explanation: No finite sample proves a universal; n = 40 gives 40² + 40 + 41 = 41², composite.
medium.deepDive: Universals (∀n …) quantify over infinitely many n; examples only witness instances. A single counterexample falsifies, but no finite stock verifies. Here n = 40 (and n = 41) expose compositeness. More examples (option B) never cross the finite/infinite gap. Primality is checkable per-n — the issue is generalization, not checking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No finite count suffices — even a million cases leave infinitely many unchecked.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Each instance is checkable (e.g., 3²+3+41 = 53, prime); generalization is the problem.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cases 3–5 are consistent with, but never prove, the infinite universal.

medium.prompt: Which establishes 'for every integer n, n² + n is even'?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Factor n(n+1): one of n, n+1 is even, so the product is even.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Note that n² + n looks even.

medium.hint: Next step: look for reasoning that covers EVERY n at once — not just sampled values.
medium.explanation: Consecutive integers always include an even one, so n(n+1) is even for all n.
medium.deepDive: The factorization argument is general: for arbitrary n, exactly one of n, n+1 is even, and even-times-anything is even. It uses no facts specific to small n. Options B and D sample finitely many cases — consistent but unproven. Option C is an impression, not an argument. Generality is what promotes evidence to proof.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Three cases never cover the infinite universal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 'Looks even' is not a reason covering every n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One large case is still one case, not all integers.

medium.prompt: To refute 'all swans are white', what suffices?

choices.label: B
choices.body: A proof that most swans are white.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A proof that no swans exist.

medium.hint: Next step: negate the universal — what existential claim must be witnessed?
medium.explanation: ¬∀x(Swan(x)→White(x)) ≡ ∃x(Swan(x)∧¬White(x)): one counterexample refutes.
medium.deepDive: Universals are strong (claim about every case) so their negations are weak (need just one failure). A single black swan exhibits Swan∧¬White, falsifying the universal. Confirming instances (options B, C) never refute. Proving no swans exist would make the universal vacuously true — the opposite of refuting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Confirming most cases is consistent with the universal, not a refutation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A positive instance supports but cannot refute a universal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Empty swan-domain makes 'all swans are white' vacuously true.

medium.prompt: ¬∀x F(x) is logically equivalent to…
medium.hint: Next step: push ¬ past ∀ — flip the quantifier and negate the body.
medium.explanation: 'Not everything is F' means 'something is non-F'.
medium.deepDive: Negating a universal yields an existential of the negation: a universal fails via one counterexample, and that witness is exactly what ∃x¬F(x) asserts. Keeping ∀ (option B) gives ¬∃…-strength ('nothing is F') — too strong. Dropping the inner ¬ (option D) forgets to negate the body. ¬∃xF(x) is the dual law's other side (≡ ∀x¬F(x)).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is ¬∃x F(x) ('nothing is F') — stronger than 'not everything'.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is ∀x ¬F(x) — again 'nothing is F', too strong.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That drops the inner negation — 'something is F' differs from 'something is non-F'.

medium.prompt: ¬∃x F(x) is logically equivalent to…
medium.hint: Next step: push ¬ past ∃ — flip the quantifier and negate the body.
medium.explanation: 'Nothing is F' means 'everything is non-F'.
medium.deepDive: Denying existence forces universal absence: if no witness is F, each element must be non-F. Keeping ∃ (option B) gives 'something is non-F' — compatible with other Fs existing, far weaker. ¬∀xF(x) is 'not everything is F' (option C's content) — also weaker. ∀xF(x) is the opposite extreme. Flip-plus-negate is the full two-move rule.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is ¬∀x F(x) ('not everything') — weaker, allowing other Fs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is ∃x ¬F(x) — one non-F, not universal absence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is the opposite: everything IS F.

medium.prompt: "Not every bird flies" (B(x): bird, F(x): flies). Best symbolization?
medium.hint: Next step: negate ∀x(B(x)→F(x)) — flip ∀ to ∃, then fix the body with the ¬(P→Q) rule.
medium.explanation: Negation gives ∃x¬(B→F) ≡ ∃x(B∧¬F): a non-flying bird exists (penguin).
medium.deepDive: Two moves: quantifier flip (∀→∃) plus body negation ¬(B→F) ≡ B∧¬F. The witness must be a genuine bird AND flightless — ∧ restricts correctly. ∀ versions claim about all birds. The →-existential (option D) is witnessed by any non-bird (a rock), proving nothing about birds. Penguin is the intended witness.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That says every bird is flightless — far stronger than 'not every'.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That says no bird flies — the 'nothing is F' extreme, too strong.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Any non-bird (a rock, F→… = T) spuriously witnesses this — wrong restrictor.

medium.prompt: "There is no largest integer" (domain integers). Best symbolization?
medium.hint: Next step: negate 'a largest exists' ∃x∀y(x≥y) — flip each quantifier in turn.
medium.explanation: ¬∃x∀y(x≥y) ≡ ∀x∃y¬(x≥y) ≡ ∀x∃y(y>x): every integer has a bigger one.
medium.deepDive: 'Largest exists' = ∃x∀y(x≥y): some x beats-or-ties all y. Negating flips ∃→∀ and ∀→∃, and ¬(x≥y) ≡ (y>x). Result: for each x some y exceeds it. Option B is the un-negated 'largest exists' — the opposite. ∀∀ overclaims (every y beats every x). ∃∃ merely says some pair is ordered — trivially true, proving nothing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That asserts a largest integer exists — the claim being denied.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That says every y exceeds every x — impossible (take y = x).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That says some pair is ordered — true but far weaker than 'no largest'.

medium.prompt: ∀x ∃y R(x, y) and ∃y ∀x R(x, y) differ in that the second…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Requires a single y that works for every x.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Is logically equivalent to the first.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Cannot be expressed in first-order logic.

medium.hint: Next step: ask who is chosen first — does y get to depend on x, or must one y serve all?
medium.explanation: 'Some y works for all x' is strictly stronger than 'for each x, some y'.
medium.deepDive: In ∀x∃y, y is chosen after x — it may vary with x (each person has some mother). In ∃y∀x, y is fixed first and must suit every x (someone is everyone's mother). So ∃∀ implies ∀∃ but not conversely. With R(x,y) = 'y is x's mother' on people: ∀∃ true, ∃∀ false. Order is dependence structure, not decoration.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The mother example separates them: ∀∃ true, ∃∀ false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: It depends on R — e.g., with R(x,y) = 'y ≥ x' on naturals with fixed y = x… (take R trivially true: both hold).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both are textbook first-order formulas.

medium.prompt: Domain: people. 'Everyone loves someone' (∀x∃y Loves(x,y)) versus 'Someone is loved by everyone' (∃y∀x Loves(x,y)). Which is true if each person loves their own parent but nobody is universally loved?
medium.hint: Next step: check witnesses — does each x have a y? Is there one y for all x?
medium.explanation: Each person supplies their own loved-one (∀∃ true), but no single person is loved by all (∃∀ false).
medium.deepDive: ∀∃ needs per-x witnesses: x's parent works for each x. ∃∀ needs a universal beloved: by hypothesis none exists. So the scenario separates them cleanly. This is the canonical ∀∃-without-∃∀ model. Collapsing the two ('order irrelevant') would wrongly predict both true or both false.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No universal beloved exists by hypothesis, so ∃∀ is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The missing universal beloved falsifies the second.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Per-x parents verify the first — it is not false.

medium.prompt: Which entailment holds between ∀x∃y R(x,y) and ∃y∀x R(x,y)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ∃y∀x R(x,y) implies ∀x∃y R(x,y), but not conversely.

choices.label: B
choices.body: ∀x∃y R(x,y) implies ∃y∀x R(x,y), but not conversely.

medium.hint: Next step: test the strong-to-weak direction — if one y suits all x, does each x have a y?
medium.explanation: A universal y works for each x (∃∀→∀∃); per-x witnesses need not coincide (∀∃⇏∃∀).
medium.deepDive: Proof of ∃∀→∀∃: fix the universal y₀ witnessing ∃∀; for arbitrary x, y₀ witnesses ∃yR(x,y). Converse fails by the mother model (∀∃ true, ∃∀ false). So the implication is strictly one-way. Equivalence (option C) ignores the counterexample. 'Neither' (option D) misses the easy forward direction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That reverses the direction — per-x witnesses need not coincide in one y.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The mother model (∀∃ true, ∃∀ false) refutes equivalence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The ∃∀→∀∃ direction always holds via the universal witness.

medium.prompt: ∀x (Cube(x) → Large(x)) with domain blocks. A counterexample needs…
medium.hint: Next step: falsify Cube→Large — which truth-value combo does that, and which block realizes it?
medium.explanation: Need Cube true with Large false: a cube that is not large.
medium.deepDive: ¬∀x(C→L) ≡ ∃x(C∧¬L): witness must be a cube AND non-large. Large tetrahedron is ¬C∧L (confirms vacuously). Small tetrahedron is ¬C∧¬L (confirms vacuously). Large cube is C∧L (confirms genuinely). Only the small cube is the C∧¬L falsifier. Counterexamples match the negated body exactly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Non-cube with Large true gives F→T = true — confirms, not refutes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Non-cube non-large gives F→F = true — confirms vacuously.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Large cube gives T→T = true — a confirming instance.

medium.prompt: "Every student passed" (domain people; S(x): student, P(x): passed). Correct symbolization?
medium.hint: Next step: ask what the claim says about non-students — must they have passed too?
medium.explanation: Non-students satisfy S→P vacuously; ∧ would wrongly demand everyone be a passing student.
medium.deepDive: ∀+→ restricts to students: non-students (S false) give F→… = T regardless of passing. ∀+∧ claims everyone is a student who passed — refuted by any non-student. ∃+∧ says some student passed — far weaker. P→S is the converse (passers are students) — different claim, refuted by a passing non-student.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That makes every person a passing student — non-students refute it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That says some student passed — weaker than 'every'.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is the converse — all passers are students.

medium.prompt: "Some student failed" (S(x): student, P(x): passed). Correct symbolization?
medium.hint: Next step: demand a witness with both traits — student AND non-passer.
medium.explanation: Need an x that is a student and did not pass; → would admit non-students spuriously.
medium.deepDive: ∃+∧ is the existential restrictor: witness must satisfy both conjuncts. With →, any non-student (S false → F→… = T) spuriously witnesses — even if every student passed. ∀ versions universalize ('no student passed' / 'everyone is a failing student'). The ∧/→ pairing (∃↔∧) is load-bearing here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Any non-student vacuously witnesses S→¬P — proves nothing about students.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That says no student passed — stronger than 'some failed'.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That says everyone is a failing student — far stronger.

medium.prompt: Scope check: in ∀x (P(x) → ∃y Q(x, y)), which variables fall inside which quantifier?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both x's under ∀x; y under ∃y (which is itself inside ∀x).

choices.label: C
choices.body: y is free; only x is bound.

choices.label: D
choices.body: x in P(x) is free; x in Q(x,y) is bound.

medium.hint: Next step: bracket scopes outside-in — ∀x covers the whole conditional including the ∃y part.
medium.explanation: ∀x's scope is the full conditional; ∃y's scope is Q(x,y), nested inside — so x is ∀-bound everywhere, y ∃-bound.
medium.deepDive: Nesting: ∀x [ P(x) → ∃y [ Q(x,y) ] ]. The inner ∃y sits inside ∀x's scope, so y may depend on x (for each x, some y). Both x occurrences are inside ∀x — bound, undivided by the →. Swapping binders (option B) misreads nesting. y is bound (not free). Scope never splits a variable's occurrences across one connective.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nesting is outside-in: ∀x contains ∃y, not the reverse.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: y sits inside ∃y's brackets — bound, not free.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ∀x's scope covers the whole conditional — both x's are bound.

medium.prompt: "Every number has a successor" (domain naturals). Correct symbolization?
medium.hint: Next step: let the successor depend on x — which order lets y vary with x?
medium.explanation: For each x some y exceeds it (y = x+1 works); the reverse order demands one y above all.
medium.deepDive: ∀∃ gives per-x successors: given x, y = x+1 witnesses y>x. ∃∀ demands a maximum-beating y above every x — false on naturals (no largest). ∀∀ demands every y beat every x — false (take y=x). ∃∃ says some pair is ordered — true but trivial, missing 'every number'. Order encodes dependence: successor-of-x varies with x.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That asserts a largest natural — false; it is the ∃∀-stronger misreading.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Take y = x: x > x is false, so ∀∀ fails.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One ordered pair (e.g., 1 < 2) never expresses 'every number has one'.

hard.prompt: P is true, Q is false, R is true. What is (P ∧ Q) → R?

choices.label: B
choices.body: False, because P ∧ Q contains a false

choices.label: C
choices.body: False, because R is true while part of the antecedent is false

hard.hint: Next step: evaluate the parenthesized antecedent first, then apply →.
hard.explanation: P ∧ Q is false (Q is false), and any false antecedent makes the implication true.
hard.deepDive: Inside-out evaluation: P∧Q = T∧F = F. Then F → R is vacuously true regardless of R. Skipping the first step and judging by 'contains a false' misfires. Parentheses force the ∧ to finish before → is considered. Hence a partly-false antecedent still yields a true conditional here.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A false antecedent makes → true, not false — the falsity was already absorbed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mismatch between antecedent parts and R does not falsify; only T→F does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: All inputs are valued, so the compound has a definite value: true.

hard.prompt: P is true and Q is true. What is P → (Q → P)?

choices.label: B
choices.body: False, because Q → P goes backwards

choices.label: D
choices.body: True only if P caused Q

hard.hint: Next step: evaluate the inner (Q → P) first, then the outer →.
hard.explanation: Inner Q → P is T → T = true; outer P → true is T → T = true.
hard.deepDive: Right-nested → evaluates inside-out: inner (T→T) = T, then outer (T→T) = T. In fact P → (Q → P) is a tautology (weakening): a true P is implied by anything. 'Backwards' or repeated letters do not matter. Causation is irrelevant — only the T→F pattern could falsify, and it never appears.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Direction alone never falsifies; only a T→F row does, and inner is T→T.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Repetition of a letter is fine — each occurrence takes the same value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Material → needs no causal link, only truth values.

hard.prompt: P is false. What is ¬(P ∧ ¬P)?
hard.hint: Next step: evaluate the inner contradiction P ∧ ¬P first.
hard.explanation: P ∧ ¬P is always false (a contradiction), so its negation is always true.
hard.deepDive: With P false: ¬P is true, P∧¬P = F∧T = F, and ¬F = T. More generally, no proposition is both true and false, so P∧¬P fails in every row. Negating a contradiction therefore yields a tautology. This is the law of non-contradiction stated positively.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the value of the inner P ∧ ¬P, before the outer ¬ flips it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The formula disagrees with P here (P false, formula true) — it is constantly true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The formula is valued in every row — always true.

hard.prompt: Assume P → Q is true and P is true. What must be true?

choices.label: C
