choices.body: Q could be either; nothing follows

hard.hint: Next step: rule out the T→F row — with P true, which Q keeps the implication true?
hard.explanation: T → Q is true only when Q is true, so Q must be true (modus ponens).
hard.deepDive: Given P true, the implication's truth forces the T→T row, since T→F is false by hypothesis exclusion. This is modus ponens at the semantic level. Q-false would create the forbidden row. 'Nothing follows' ignores that the T→F row was ruled out by the truth of P → Q.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: T → F is false, contradicting the assumption that P → Q is true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Q-false is eliminated by the true conditional, so Q is pinned to true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P is given as true; denying it contradicts the setup.

hard.prompt: Assume P → Q is true and Q is false. What must be true?

choices.label: C
choices.body: P could be either; nothing follows

hard.hint: Next step: test P = true against Q = false — does that row keep the implication true?
hard.explanation: P → F is true only when P is false, so P must be false (modus tollens).
hard.deepDive: With Q false, P-true would make the forbidden T→F row, contradicting the true conditional. So P must be false, giving F→F = true. This semantic argument is modus tollens. 'Nothing follows' misses that P-true was eliminated. Q stays false as given.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: T → F is false, contradicting the assumed true conditional.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: P-true is ruled out by the true conditional, so P is pinned to false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Q is given as false; flipping it contradicts the setup.

hard.prompt: Assume P → Q is true and ¬P is true (P false). What follows about Q?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Nothing — Q could be true or false

hard.hint: Next step: list the rows with P false — do both keep F→Q true?
hard.explanation: Both F → T and F → F are true, so a true conditional with false P constrains nothing about Q.
hard.deepDive: Denying the antecedent is a fallacy precisely because two rows survive: F→T and F→F. The conditional rules out only T→F, which is already avoided. So Q floats free. Concluding Q-false (or Q-true) overclaims from a vacuous truth. This foreshadows the denying-the-antecedent fallacy.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is denying the antecedent — F→T is a live counterexample (e.g., sprinkler).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: F→F is a live counterexample, so Q-true is not forced either.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ¬P true means P is false by hypothesis; flipping it contradicts the setup.

hard.prompt: "If the team wins (W), the city celebrates (C)." The city is celebrating. A fan concludes the team won. What is wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Affirms the consequent — celebrations have other causes (parades, festivals)

choices.label: B
choices.body: Denies the antecedent — winning was never assumed

choices.label: C
choices.body: Uses the contrapositive — which is invalid

hard.hint: Next step: ask whether C-true forces W-true, or whether C can hold without W.
hard.explanation: W → C with C true does not force W true; other causes can produce C.
hard.deepDive: This is affirming the consequent: W→C, C ∴ W. The T→T and F→T rows both keep the conditional true with C true, so W floats. A festival (W false, C true) is the counterexample. Only the contrapositive (¬C ∴ ¬W) would be valid here. Conflating C→W with W→C is the converse error.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nothing was denied here; the fan affirmed C, the consequent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The contrapositive (¬C → ¬W) is valid — but the fan did not use it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The F→T row (festival, no win) keeps premises true with a false conclusion.

hard.prompt: P → Q is true and P → ¬Q is true. What must hold?
hard.hint: Next step: suppose P were true — what would Q have to be to keep BOTH conditionals true?
hard.explanation: If P were true, Q would have to be both true and false — impossible — so P is false.
hard.deepDive: Suppose P true: first conditional forces Q true (T→T), second forces Q false (T→F fails unless Q false... actually P→¬Q with P true needs ¬Q true, i.e., Q false). Contradiction, so P cannot be true. Hence P is false, making both conditionals vacuously true. This mini-reductio previews proof by contradiction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: P-true would demand Q both true and false at once — impossible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: With P false, Q floats free (both F→T and F→F hold), so Q is not pinned.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P-true is ruled out, so P-false does follow.

hard.prompt: Every member of an empty club is a astronaut. This claim is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Vacuously true — there is no member to serve as a counterexample

choices.label: B
choices.body: False — nobody in it is an astronaut

choices.label: C
choices.body: Meaningless — empty subjects cannot be judged

choices.label: D
choices.body: True only if astronauts exist somewhere

hard.hint: Next step: search for a counterexample member — can you find one in an empty club?
hard.explanation: A universal over an empty domain has no counterexample, so it is vacuously true.
hard.deepDive: Universals ('every member is…') fail only via counterexamples. With no members, the falsifying row (member who is not an astronaut) cannot occur — exactly like F→Q. So the claim is true regardless of astronauts elsewhere. Existence claims ('there is a member who…') over empty domains go the other way: false.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Falsity needs an actual non-astronaut member; none exists here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Empty-domain universals have a definite value: true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Vacuous truth needs no outside witnesses — absence of counterexamples suffices.

hard.prompt: P → Q and ¬P ∨ Q have the same truth table. Therefore they are…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unrelated — sameness of tables proves nothing

hard.hint: Next step: recall the definition — same value in every row means what?
hard.explanation: Sharing all truth values across rows is exactly logical equivalence.
hard.deepDive: Equivalence (≡) is defined as row-for-row agreement: φ ≡ ψ iff every valuation gives them the same value. P→Q and ¬P∨Q both fail only on T/F, so they are equivalent. Contradictories would disagree in every row. Neither is a tautology (each fails once). Same-table is the whole test, not a hint.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Opposites disagree everywhere; these agree everywhere.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Each fails in the T/F row, so neither is all-true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Row-for-row agreement is the definition of equivalence.

hard.prompt: Are P → Q and Q → P logically equivalent?

choices.label: A
choices.body: No — they differ in rows T/F and F/T

choices.label: C
choices.body: Yes — both are contingencies with three true rows

choices.label: D
choices.body: No — one is a tautology and the other is not

hard.hint: Next step: compare the mixed rows — where does each one falsify?
hard.explanation: P→Q fails on T/F where Q→P holds, and vice versa on F/T, so the tables differ.
hard.deepDive: P→Q is F only at (T,F); Q→P is F only at (F,T). They agree on (T,T) and (F,F) but cross on the mixed rows. Sharing a true-count (3 each) does not make them equivalent — the false rows sit in different places. Implication is directional; only the contrapositive (¬Q→¬P) matches P→Q.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Implication is directional — the converse has a different table.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Equal true-counts do not imply equal tables; the false rows differ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Neither is a tautology — each fails once, in different rows.

hard.prompt: Which pair is logically equivalent?
hard.hint: Next step: check the F/F row — which options survive 'both false' alongside ↔?
hard.explanation: ↔ is true on T/T and F/F; only the conjunction of both directions matches both rows.
hard.deepDive: P↔Q demands matching values: T on (T,T) and (F,F), F on mixed rows. (P→Q)∧(Q→P) enforces each direction, failing exactly on the mixed rows — same table. P∧Q drops the F/F row. P∨Q adds the mixed rows. ¬(P↔Q) is the exact opposite (true on mixed rows only).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: P ∧ Q is false in row F/F where P ↔ Q is true.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: P ∨ Q is true in mixed rows where P ↔ Q is false.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A formula is never equivalent to its own negation.

hard.prompt: Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) expresses a formula as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A conjunction of disjunctions of literals

choices.label: B
choices.body: A disjunction of conjunctions of literals

hard.hint: Next step: parse the name — 'conjunctive' (outer ∧) of 'disjunctions' (inner ∨).
hard.explanation: CNF is an AND of ORs of literals, e.g., (P ∨ ¬Q) ∧ (R ∨ S).
hard.deepDive: CNF = outer conjunction, inner disjunctions, innermost literals (atoms or negated atoms). It is the input format for SAT solvers and resolution. Swapping the two levels gives DNF (OR of ANDs). Single-implication or biconditional shapes do not generalize — any formula converts to CNF, possibly with new variables.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That swaps the levels — it is Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Implication chains cannot express arbitrary formulas without rewriting.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Biconditionals of atoms cover only a fragment of formulas.

hard.prompt: Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) expresses a formula as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A disjunction of conjunctions of literals

choices.label: B
choices.body: A conjunction of disjunctions of literals

hard.hint: Next step: parse the name — 'disjunctive' (outer ∨) of 'conjunctions' (inner ∧).
hard.explanation: DNF is an OR of ANDs of literals, e.g., (P ∧ ¬Q) ∨ (R ∧ S).
hard.deepDive: DNF mirrors CNF with levels swapped: outer ∨, inner ∧, literals inside. Each disjunct names a satisfying-row pattern (which atoms are true/false), so DNF is read off directly from the true rows of a table. The CNF option reverses the levels. Bare negations and Horn clauses are unrelated fragments.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That reverses the levels — it is Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A single negated conjunction is just one clause shape, not the general form.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Horn clauses are a tractable CNF fragment, not DNF.

hard.prompt: Which is in CNF (conjunction of disjunctions of literals)?
hard.hint: Next step: check the outer connective first — CNF must join clauses with ∧.
hard.explanation: Outer ∧ joins two ∨-clauses of literals — exactly CNF.
hard.deepDive: Verify level by level: outer ∧ ✓, each clause an ∨ of literals (P, Q / ¬P, R) ✓. Option B has outer ∨ (DNF instead). The implication hides a ¬P∨… structure but is not literally an AND of ORs. ¬(P∨Q) has the negation outside a disjunction — pushing it in gives ¬P∧¬Q, a single CNF clause, but as written it is not in CNF.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Outer ∨ with inner ∧ is DNF, the level-swapped form.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: An implication is not literally an AND of ORs until rewritten.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The un-pushed negation over ∨ violates the literal/clause layering.

hard.prompt: Which formula has the same truth table as P ↔ ¬Q?
hard.hint: Next step: ask when P ↔ ¬Q is true — matching or mismatching P and Q?
hard.explanation: P ↔ ¬Q is true exactly when P and Q differ, which is precisely ¬(P↔Q).
hard.deepDive: ↔ reports agreement, so P↔¬Q reports agreement-with-negation = disagreement: true on (T,F) and (F,T), false on (T,T) and (F,F). That is the row-complement of P↔Q (true on agreement rows), hence ¬(P↔Q). P→Q is true in three rows; P∧¬Q in one; P∨Q in three different rows — none match the two-mismatch pattern.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: P → Q is true in three rows; P ↔ ¬Q in only two.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: P ∧ ¬Q holds only on (T,F); P ↔ ¬Q also holds on (F,T).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P ∨ Q is true on (T,T) where P ↔ ¬Q is false.

hard.prompt: P ↔ Q is true in exactly which rows?

choices.label: A
choices.body: T/T and F/F (P and Q agree)

choices.label: C
choices.body: T/F and F/T (P and Q differ)

hard.hint: Next step: test agreement — ↔ is the 'same value?' detector.
hard.explanation: The biconditional is true when both sides match: both true or both false.
hard.deepDive: ↔ ≡ (P→Q)∧(Q→P): the mixed rows each falsify one direction, leaving only agreement rows true. 'T/T only' describes ∧; 'mixed rows' describes exclusive-or (¬(P↔Q)); 'all rows' would be a tautology. ↔ is contingent with a 2T/2F split.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is P ∧ Q — ↔ additionally accepts F/F.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is exclusive-or, the negation of ↔.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mixed rows falsify ↔, so it is not a tautology.

hard.prompt: Which is logically equivalent to ¬(P ↔ Q)?
hard.hint: Next step: list the disagreement rows — each needs its own conjunction, joined by ∨.
hard.explanation: ¬(P↔Q) holds on the two mismatch rows, named by (P∧¬Q) and (¬P∧Q).
hard.deepDive: This is DNF read off the table: true rows (T,F) and (F,T) become conjunctions joined by ∨. Option B names the agreement rows — that is P↔Q itself. P→Q has three true rows, P∨Q three different ones. Enumerating true rows into disjuncts is the general table-to-DNF recipe.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That names the agreement rows — it is P ↔ Q itself, the opposite.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: P → Q is true in three rows, but ¬(P↔Q) in only two.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P ∨ Q is true on (T,T) where ¬(P↔Q) is false.

hard.prompt: Goal: prove 'if n² is even, then n is even'. The cleanest strategy is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Contrapositive: assume n is odd, show n² is odd.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Direct: assume n² is even, take square roots.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Assume n² is even and n is even, then conclude.

hard.hint: Next step: ask which side is easier to work with — even square roots or odd arithmetic?
hard.explanation: Odd n = 2k+1 gives n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, odd — the contrapositive proves the original.
hard.deepDive: Direct proof stalls: from n² = 2m there is no clean integer formula for n. Contrapositive flips to oddness, which has the workable form 2k+1 with easy squaring. Examples (option C) never prove the universal. Assuming the conclusion (option D) is circular. Strategy choice = picking the direction with algebraic traction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Evenness of n² gives no direct formula for n — square roots need not be integers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Finite examples never prove the infinite universal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Assuming what must be proved is circular reasoning.

hard.prompt: Goal: prove 'there are infinitely many primes'. The classic strategy is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Contradiction: assume finitely many, multiply them plus one, find a new prime factor.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Direct: write a formula listing all primes.

hard.hint: Next step: suppose the opposite (a complete finite list) — can you build a number escaping it?
hard.explanation: Euclid: given p₁…pₖ, N = p₁⋯pₖ+1 has a prime factor outside the list — contradiction.
hard.deepDive: Assume finitely many primes p₁…pₖ. N = product + 1 leaves remainder 1 on division by each pᵢ, so no pᵢ divides N; N's prime factor is new — contradicting completeness. No direct listing formula exists (option B). Contrapositive adds nothing here. Finite lists (option D) are consistent with finiteness, proving nothing about infinity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: No such complete listing formula exists — that is what is being proved impossible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Contrapositive of a finiteness claim gives no constructive escape like N does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Any finite list is compatible with 'those are all' — no contradiction arises.

hard.prompt: Goal: prove 'if P then Q' where Q's negation is easy to work with but P is awkward. Best strategy?

choices.label: D
choices.body: Give one example with P and Q both true.

hard.hint: Next step: pick the equivalent formulation whose antecedent (¬Q) has traction.
hard.explanation: Contrapositive is equivalent to the original, and starts from workable ¬Q.
hard.deepDive: Since (P→Q) ≡ (¬Q→¬P), proving either proves both — choose the one with usable hypotheses. Affirming Q (option B) is the converse fallacy. Denying P (option C) is the inverse fallacy. One example (option D) never proves a universal conditional. Strategy = valid rephrasing toward traction, never fallacy or sampling.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That proves the converse Q → P, not equivalent to P → Q.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That proves the inverse ¬P → ¬Q, not equivalent to P → Q.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One T→T instance never proves the whole conditional.

hard.prompt: A countermodel to an argument is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: An interpretation where all premises are true and the conclusion is false.

choices.label: B
choices.body: An interpretation where all premises are false.

choices.label: C
choices.body: An interpretation where the conclusion is true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Any model of the conclusion alone.

hard.hint: Next step: build the ONE banned row — premises true, conclusion false.
hard.explanation: A single true-premises/false-conclusion interpretation proves invalidity.
hard.deepDive: Validity bans exactly the T-premises/F-conclusion combination, so exhibiting it refutes validity at once. False premises (option B) are compatible with validity. True conclusions (options C, D) say nothing — validity constrains what happens WHEN premises hold. One countermodel kills; no number of confirming models proves.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: False premises are compatible with validity — the banned combo needs true premises.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Conclusion truth alone constrains nothing about the premises-conclusion link.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Models of the conclusion ignore the premises entirely.

hard.prompt: Argument: 'If Ana is in Calgary (C) she is in Alberta (A). Ana is in Alberta. So Ana is in Calgary.' Countermodel?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ana in Edmonton: C→A true, A true, C false.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ana outside Alberta: premises true, conclusion false.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ana in Calgary but outside Alberta.

hard.hint: Next step: find an Alberta city that is not Calgary — keep premises true, break the conclusion.
hard.explanation: Edmonton keeps C→A true (F→T) and A true while C is false: true premises, false conclusion.
hard.deepDive: This is affirming the consequent (C→A, A ∴ C). Edmonton is the F→T row: C false, A true, conditional vacuously true. Both premises true, conclusion false — invalidity demonstrated. Option B confirms (all true). Option C makes C→A vacuously true but A false — wrong combo. Option D is impossible (Calgary entails Alberta).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: All-true confirms the premises but does not test validity — need false conclusion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Here premise A is false, so the banned true-premises combo is not built.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Calgary-without-Alberta is impossible, and would falsify C→A anyway.

hard.prompt: Why does one countermodel prove invalidity but one confirming instance never prove validity?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Validity is a universal claim over interpretations; one counterexample falsifies it.

hard.hint: Next step: parse 'valid' as 'for EVERY interpretation…' — what does it take to break a 'for every'?
hard.explanation: Valid = no countermodel exists anywhere; exhibiting one falsifies the universal, while one clean case leaves infinitely many unchecked.
hard.deepDive: Validity quantifies universally: ∀ interpretations (premises-true → conclusion-true). Its negation is existential: ∃ interpretation (premises-true ∧ conclusion-false) — witnessed by one countermodel. Confirming instances are ∃-evidence, which never establishes ∀. This is the same logic as swans: one black swan refutes 'all white'; white swans never prove it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The asymmetry is logical (∀ vs ∃), not rhetorical.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Confirming instances are fine evidence — just insufficient for a universal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Validity concerns all interpretations, not actual truth (that is soundness).

hard.prompt: Γ ⊨ φ (φ is a logical consequence of Γ) means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every model making all of Γ true also makes φ true.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Some model makes Γ and φ all true together.

choices.label: C
choices.body: φ is provable from Γ in some proof system.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Γ and φ have the same truth table.

hard.hint: Next step: read ⊨ as 'no countermodel' — every Γ-true model must satisfy φ.
hard.explanation: Semantic entailment = truth-preservation across all models.
hard.deepDive: ⊨ is validity generalized to premise sets: Γ ⊨ φ iff no interpretation makes Γ true with φ false. 'Some model' (option B) is joint satisfiability — far weaker. Provability (option C) is syntactic ⊢, which matches ⊨ only via soundness/completeness. Same-table (option D) is equivalence of two formulas, not consequence from a set.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is satisfiability of Γ ∪ {φ}, compatible with a countermodel elsewhere.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is syntactic consequence (⊢); ⊨ is its semantic counterpart.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Same-table is mutual entailment of two formulas, not consequence from premises.

hard.prompt: {P → Q, ¬Q} ⊨ ¬P holds because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: In every row with P→Q true and ¬Q true, P is false.

choices.label: B
choices.body: In some row all three formulas are true.

hard.hint: Next step: filter rows to those satisfying both premises — what is P's value in each survivor?
hard.explanation: Only row F/F satisfies both premises, and there ¬P is true — no countermodel exists.
hard.deepDive: Filter: ¬Q keeps rows (T,F), (F,F). P→Q keeps (T,T), (F,T), (F,F). Intersection: only (F,F). There ¬P is true. Since every premises-true row has ¬P true, entailment holds. 'Some row' (option B) states satisfiability, not preservation. ¬P is the conclusion, not a premise. P→Q is contingent, not a tautology.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One clean row never rules out a countermodel elsewhere — check ALL premises-true rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ¬P is the conclusion being tested, not a given premise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P → Q fails on T/F, so it is contingent — entailment still holds via filtering.

hard.prompt: {P → Q, Q} ⊨ P fails because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Row F→T makes both premises true with P false — a countermodel.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No row makes both premises true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Q is false in every premises-true row.

hard.hint: Next step: hunt for premises-true with P false — check the F→T row.
hard.explanation: Row P=false, Q=true satisfies P→Q (vacuously) and Q, yet P is false.
hard.deepDive: Filtering: Q keeps (T,T), (F,T); P→Q keeps (T,T), (F,T), (F,F); intersection (T,T), (F,T). In (F,T) the conclusion P is false — countermodel found, so entailment fails. This is affirming-the-consequent at the ⊨ level. Option B is wrong (two rows qualify). P→Q is contingent. Q is true (not false) in premises-true rows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Two rows (T/T, F/T) satisfy both premises — the issue is P failing in one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: P → Q is true in three rows — contingent, not contradictory.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Q is given true; it is P that fails in the (F,T) row.

hard.prompt: From ∀x F(x), what may you conclude for a particular term c?

choices.label: D
choices.body: Nothing — universals never apply to instances.

hard.hint: Next step: a universal covers every instance — drop ∀ and plug in c.
hard.explanation: UI: what holds of everything holds of anything — infer F(c) for any term c.
hard.deepDive: Universal instantiation (∀-elimination) moves from general to particular: ∀xF(x) ⊢ F(c). No freshness side-condition — any term works, since the universal already covers it. Option B contradicts the premise (∀ and ∃¬ are opposites). ¬F(c) reverses polarity. 'Nothing' misses that UI is the workhorse connecting quantified premises to concrete reasoning.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ∀xF(x) contradicts ∃x¬F(x) — they cannot both follow.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That negates instead of instantiating — wrong polarity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Applying universals to instances (UI) is the standard ∀-rule.

hard.prompt: From ∃x F(x), you may assume F(c) for a FRESH constant c in order to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Name an unknown witness without smuggling in extra facts about it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Reuse an old constant so the proof stays short.

hard.hint: Next step: ask why 'fresh' — what goes wrong if c already has commitments?
hard.explanation: EI introduces a temporary name for some witness; freshness prevents importing facts the witness may lack.
hard.deepDive: Existential instantiation: from ∃xF(x), suppose c with F(c) for fresh c, reason generally, then discharge. Freshness is soundness-critical: reusing 'a' (say, known even) when ∃xOdd(x) is given would 'prove' an even odd number. EI never yields ∀ (one witness ≠ all). Reuse destroys the arbitrariness the rule needs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: One witness never licenses a universal — that needs generality, not existence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Reusing constants is exactly what freshness forbids — it over-specifies the witness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: F(c) is assumed, not negated — polarity is positive.

hard.prompt: From F(c) for an ARBITRARY c (no special assumptions about c), you may conclude…
hard.hint: Next step: check arbitrariness — if the proof used nothing special about c, it works for all.
hard.explanation: UG: a proof for arbitrary c generalizes — c's anonymity means every element qualifies.
hard.deepDive: Universal generalization (∀-introduction) is the mirror of UI: UI goes ∀→instance, UG goes arbitrary-instance→∀. The proviso (c absent from assumptions and conclusion-template) guarantees c stood for 'any'. If c had special facts (c even, c in premises), generalization is blocked. ∃¬/¬∀ contradict F(c). 'Nothing' undervalues UG — it is how all ∀-theorems are proved.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: F(c) for arbitrary c supports ∀, not the existence of a counterexample.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That denies the universal — opposite of what arbitrary-c reasoning shows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Arbitrary-c reasoning is exactly what licenses ∀-conclusions (UG).

hard.prompt: To prove ∀n ≥ 0, P(n) by induction, the FIRST setup step is…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Prove P(k) for all k at once directly.

hard.hint: Next step: anchor the domino chain — which case starts it with no predecessors?
hard.explanation: Base case P(0) grounds the induction; the step then propagates it upward.
hard.deepDive: Induction = anchor + propagation. Base P(0) holds outright (no assumptions). Inductive step: ∀k(P(k)→P(k+1)) lifts truth rung by rung. Assuming P(k+1) to get P(k) (option B) runs the chain backwards. Proving all-at-once (option C) skips the method. Negating P(0) starts a contradiction proof, not induction. Base-first is the setup order.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The step goes forward (k → k+1), not backward — and base comes first.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Direct all-at-once proof is not induction's two-part setup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Negating the base starts contradiction, not induction.

hard.prompt: A student proves P(0) and stops, claiming ∀n P(n). What is missing?

choices.label: B
choices.body: More base cases P(1), P(2), P(3).

hard.hint: Next step: ask what links P(0) to P(1) — which implication is still unproved?
hard.explanation: Base alone anchors one rung; without the step implication, higher rungs never follow.
hard.deepDive: P(0) without ∀k(P(k)→P(k+1)) is an anchor with no chain: P(1), P(2), … remain unsupported. Extra bases (option B) add anchors but still no links — infinitely many rungs need the general step, not finitely many more bases. Counterexample checks (option C) test but never prove. 'Base suffices' is the base-case-only misconception — induction's power is the step.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Finitely many more bases still leave infinitely many rungs unlinked.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Failed searches never prove the universal — the step implication does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Base-only proves P(0), not the ∀-claim — the step is load-bearing.

hard.prompt: In the inductive step for ∀n ≥ 1, P(n), what may you assume and what must you show?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Assume P(k) for arbitrary k ≥ 1; show P(k+1).

hard.hint: Next step: state the step as an implication — antecedent assumed, consequent proved, k arbitrary.
hard.explanation: Inductive hypothesis P(k) (k arbitrary, ≥1) implies P(k+1); generalizing over k gives the step.
hard.deepDive: The step proves ∀k≥1(P(k)→P(k+1)): fix arbitrary k, assume P(k) (IH), derive P(k+1), discharge to the implication, generalize. Backward (option B) proves the converse implication — useless for climbing. Assuming the full ∀ (option C) is circular. P(1)∴P(1) (option D) is trivial, not the step. Direction (k→k+1) plus arbitrary-k are both load-bearing.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That proves P(k+1)→P(k) — the backward, useless direction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Assuming the whole universal to prove its base is circular.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: P(1)∴P(1) is trivially valid but is not the inductive step.

hard.prompt: Claim: Σ_{i=1}^{n} i = n(n+1)/2. Base case n = 1 gives…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Nothing checkable — formulas need no base.

hard.hint: Next step: plug n = 1 into both sides separately, then compare.
hard.explanation: Sum 1..1 is 1; formula gives 1·2/2 = 1 — match, base holds.
hard.deepDive: Base computation: LHS = Σ_{i=1}^{1}i = 1; RHS = 1(1+1)/2 = 1. Equality anchors the induction. n = 0 (option B) is outside the claimed range (n ≥ 1) — wrong anchor. Arithmetic slip (option C) mis-evaluates 1·2/2 as 2. 'No base' (option D) is the step-only misconception — every induction needs its anchor computed, not waved through.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The claim starts at n = 1, not n = 0 — anchor at the stated start.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 1·2/2 = 1, not 2 — arithmetic slip.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The base case must be computed explicitly in every induction.

hard.prompt: Inductive hypothesis: Σ_{i=1}^{k} i = k(k+1)/2. The NEXT step toward P(k+1) starts by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Adding (k+1) to both sides: LHS becomes Σ_{i=1}^{k+1} i.

hard.hint: Next step: extend the sum by its next term — add (k+1) to the IH equation.
hard.explanation: LHS + (k+1) is the (k+1)-sum; RHS + (k+1) simplifies to (k+1)(k+2)/2.
hard.deepDive: Computation: k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k/2 + 1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2 — exactly P(k+1)'s RHS. Adding the next term bridges IH to goal. Assuming the goal (option B) is circular. Rechecking k=1 (option C) repeats the base instead of advancing. Subtracting (option D) shrinks away from the goal. The step pattern: extend LHS, algebra RHS into goal shape.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That assumes the goal — circular; derive it from the IH instead.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The base is done — the step must advance from k to k+1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Subtracting moves away from the (k+1)-sum.

hard.prompt: Claim: 2^{n} ≥ n+1 for n ≥ 0. Base n = 0 and IH 2^{k} ≥ k+1. Finish P(k+1):

choices.label: D
choices.body: Check k = 5 as the general step.

hard.hint: Next step: split 2^{k+1} as 2·2^{k}, apply the IH to one factor, then compare 2(k+1) with k+2.
hard.explanation: Doubling the IH gives 2(k+1) = (k+2)+k ≥ k+2 since k ≥ 0.
hard.deepDive: Full chain: 2^{k+1} = 2·2^{k} ≥ 2(k+1) [IH, doubling preserves ≥] = k+2+k ≥ k+2 [k≥0]. Base n=0: 1 ≥ 1 ✓. Option B mis-splits exponentials (2^{k+1} ≠ 2^{k}+1). Option C proves a weaker goal (k+1 instead of k+2). Option D samples instead of generalizing. Exponential steps need the ×2 structure used, not +1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 2^{k+1} = 2·2^{k}, not 2^{k}+1 — exponentials double, not increment.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Goal is ≥ k+2, not ≥ k+1 — this under-proves by one.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: One numeric case never proves the ∀k step.
